questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)={t}^{3}-6{t}^{2},\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-6{t}^{2}) \\  & =3{t}^{2}-12t\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}-12t) \\  & =6t-12\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =6t-12 \\ 6t & =12 \\ t & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t=2.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
v(2)=3(2)^{2}-12(2)=-12.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Intervals of Increasing or Decreasing Displacement
questions.problem:
The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)=(4t-7){e}^{t},$ where $t>0$ is the time, measured in seconds. Find the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x.$

$t\in (${{field-1}},

{{field-2}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of increasing $x,$ then its velocity is positive. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((4t-7){e}^{t}) \\  & =4{e}^{t}+(4t-7){e}^{t} \\  & =(4t-3){e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x$, we solve $v(t)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & >0 \\ (4t-3){e}^{t} & >0 \\ 4t-3 & >0 \\ t & >\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of increasing $x$ is 

$$
t\in (\frac{3}{4},\infty ).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Intervals of Increasing or Decreasing Displacement
questions.problem:
The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)=\sqrt{t}\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡t-2),$ where $t>0$ is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x.$

$t\in (${{field-1}},

{{field-2}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of increasing $x,$ then its velocity is positive. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\,(\sqrt{t}\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡t-2)) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t-2}{2\sqrt{t}}+\sqrt{t}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t-2}{2\sqrt{t}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{2\sqrt{t}}-\frac{2}{2\sqrt{t}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{2\sqrt{t}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{2\sqrt{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x$, we solve the inequality $v(t)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & >0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{2\sqrt{t}} & >0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t & >0 \\ t & >{e}^{0} \\ t & >1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the time interval in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x$ is 

$$
t\in (1,\infty ).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Intervals of Increasing or Decreasing Displacement
questions.problem:
The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by 
$s(t)=(4t-12)^{2},$
where $t\ge 0$ is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x.$

$t\in [${{field-1}},

{{field-2}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of decreasing $x,$ then its velocity is negative.

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\,((4t-12)^{2}) \\  & =8(4t-12) \\  & =32(t-3)\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we solve the inequality $v(t)<0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & <0 \\ 32(t-3) & <0 \\ t-3 & <0 \\ t & <3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the time interval in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x$ is

$$
t\in [0,\,3).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}ln\,({t}^{2}),\,t>0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.

The acceleration is zero at $t=$
{{field-1}}, and the velocity at this moment is
$v=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}ln\,({t}^{2})=2{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\,(2{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2(2t)\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+2{t}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & =4t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+2t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+2t) \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+4t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+2 \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a(t)=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+6 & =0 \\ 4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-6 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ t & ={e}^{-3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t={e}^{-3/2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v\,({e}^{-3/2}) & ={e}^{-3/2}(4ln\,({e}^{-3/2})+2) \\  & ={e}^{-3/2}(4\cdot (-\frac{3}{2})+2) \\  & ={e}^{-3/2}(-6+2) \\  & =-4{e}^{-3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration is zero at $t={e}^{-3/2},$ and the velocity at this moment is $v=-4{e}^{-3/2}.$
